claims.text: Resistance to combined wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the ability to form a rapidly reforming, adherent passive oxide film on a nanocrystalline surface.
Grain refinement increases surface hardness and thereby reduces wear.
A high density of grain boundaries provides active sites that accelerate passive-film regeneration after mechanical damage.
A coarse-grained CoCrFeNi alloy does not inherently promote rapid passive-film formation.
A controlled microalloying addition or thermomechanical treatment can refine the grain structure and enhance formation of a protective, self-healing passive oxide.
Passive-film formation is thermodynamically favored in chloride-containing media at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
A nanocrystalline microstructure enhances hardness and promotes the continuity of a self-healing passive film along grain boundaries.
During wear, increased grain-boundary area accelerates local oxidation so that mechanically removed passive film reforms rapidly.
Continuous passive-film damage and repair prevents corrosive species from reaching the substrate and limits degradation.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, the modified HEA will have a lower wear rate than the baseline.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, the modified HEA will have a lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
The modified HEA will experience less total material loss under combined wear and corrosion than the baseline.
Differences between modified and baseline alloys will be modest in isolated wear or corrosion tests but substantially larger under simultaneous wear and corrosion.
A conventionally processed, compositionally similar baseline will have a coarser microstructure and a less stable passive film.
The proposed benefit should occur in neutral to mildly acidic chloride solutions at ambient to moderate temperatures when the passive film remains stable.
Very high chloride concentration, excessive mechanical load, or film-destabilizing temperature can overwhelm passive-film formation and healing and eliminate the benefit.
Boron doping can modify coating microstructure and substantially improve both wear and corrosion resistance.
A CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA coating adhered to stainless steel and exhibited corrosion resistance during a six-hour test in 3.5 wt% NaCl at room temperature.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits a microalloying addition, but the experimental design requires the treated and baseline specimens to have identical bulk compositions. Those requirements are incompatible if microalloying is the selected intervention, though they are compatible if only thermomechanical processing is used.
